title: Bebop, Parker and Gillespie's audition for Kirby, the shuffle
summary: He was never tuned to Bebop; Parker and Dizzy auditioned for Kirby, whose style was a shuffle; Louis Jordan the first Rock group.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, look. After Teddy Wilson...and we mentioned Bebop. Now, who are the first Bebop pianists that you are conscious of, that you ran up against?
What do you mean?
When Bebop was coming in did you hear Monk or Bud Powell first, or...?
Well, I was never really too tuned to it too much, you know.
You weren't.
No.
But you were conscious of it.
Oh, definitely. This is nothing new to me.
Ramirez - 192
No, it wasn't.

I remember Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie auditioned for John Kirby's orchestra, but it wasn't their style. Kirby's was mostly a shuffle rhythm type of thing, while Charlie Parker and Dizzy were playing something else. Now, the shuffle is very important. It has a backbeat to it, it's a variation, and for the Blues it's effective.
Even in later years I always noticed with Duke's band when Sam Woodyard would start to play a shuffle rhythm... It really used to work with that band.
Oh yeah. And Louis Jordan was the first so-called Rock group, to me, that ever existed. It was very popular. Louis Jordan was ahead of his time.
But yet shuffle rhythm was always referred to... For a long time people would speak of it with contempt, wouldn't they?
Well, they would, I suppose. But actually, what more contemptuous music do you have than in the Rock, so-called Rock Era, playing that DUM-DUM-DUM/DUM-DUM-DUM...
Oh, I know. I know.
See what I mean? That was a disgrace.
What I meant was that the Jazz musicians sort of referred to shuffle rhythm as though it was something...
Sure, I remember. There was an antiquated
Ramirez - 193
sort of view. Well, I think every period back at something they've done as...
